translations.note: Diaciminum is the name of an apothecary's confection made from cumin (Greek dia, 'made of' + kyminon).
Dianisum is the name of a confection made from aniseed.
Diacinnamonum is the name of a confection made from cinnamon. The following words 'cold, as' begin Burton's next category and do not render this name.
An official book of drug formulas and their preparation, such as the London Pharmacopoeia of 1618.
This is the unguentum alabastrinum, a cooling ointment made with powdered alabaster.

A famous opiate electuary named after its inventor Philo of Tarsus, as Burton's next words explain ('which ... Philonius a Roman long since composed'). It is the name of a compound medicine, not a quotation.
The theriac (in English 'treacle'), a compound antidote attributed to Andromachus, Nero's physician. Galen wrote about it and revised it. This is the name of a medicine, not a quotation.

Diambra is the apothecaries' name (from Greek dia, 'made of', and ambra) for an aromatic confection made with ambergris. Medium confidence because 'ambra' could also be read as amber, but ambergris was the usual ingredient.
Dianthus is the apothecaries' name (Greek dia anthos, 'of flowers') for a cordial confection. In pharmacy 'anthos' usually meant rosemary flowers, the main ingredient.
Diagalinga is the apothecaries' name for a warming confection based on galingale root.
Diazinziber is the apothecaries' name (dia + zingiber) for a confection of ginger.
Diacapers is the apothecaries' name for a confection of capers. Capers were traditionally prescribed for the spleen.
This is apparently Diacorallion, a cooling confection of coral. Burton's spelling 'Diacorolli' is irregular.
Diarrhodon Abbatis is a standard cooling confection of roses, traditionally ascribed to an abbot.
Diacodion is the apothecaries' name (Greek kōdeia, 'poppy head') for a sleep-inducing syrup or confection of poppy heads.

The Latin adverb crasse means 'grossly, without refinement'. Burton's point is that these compounds are crudely put together, like the rest. The word could also be read as an English 'crass' spelling.
